children: Over the past 25 years, Indian agriculture has undergone a foundational shift largely driven by investments in irrigation, rural infrastructure, farm technology and direct grower support. Under Narendra Modi’s leadership, first in Gujarat and later at the Centre, strengthening rural livelihoods has remained central to India’s development trajectory. This productive capacity is reflected in the nation’s food grain output, which reached an estimated record of 357.73 million tonne in 2024-25.

The next chapter of this journey requires a broader benchmark of success. While national food security remains fundamental, agricultural progress must also translate into sustainable farm incomes, healthier soils, disciplined water use and greater economic resilience for the smallholder.
Gujarat’s experience: Development through ground-level action

Gujarat’s agrarian turnaround offers valuable lessons on how water governance, rural infrastructure and community engagement can strengthen agricultural productivity in arid regions. Measures such as water conservation, combining the Sardar Sarovar canal work with decentralised check dams, farm ponds and micro-irrigation, helped alleviate chronic water scarcity across the State. Alongside water infrastructure, the Jyotigram Yojana and Krishi Mahotsav brought agricultural scientists directly to village doorsteps before the sowing season.

The grassroots principle of khet ka pani khet mein, gaon ka pani gaon mein (retaining field water in the field and village water in the village) captures a lasting truth: water security begins with local resource management.

Subsequent national programmes supporting micro-irrigation under PMKSY, direct income liquidity via PM-KISAN, and crop risk insurance have further expanded the scope of this agriculture across India. The priority now is ensuring that macro-level infrastructure consistently translates into better farm-gate decisions.
Beyond production: The farmer income imperative
Today, the central challenge facing Indian agriculture is no longer simply producing more; It is about ensuring that higher output generates remunerative and sustainable net returns.

Fragmented landholdings, rising cultivation costs, mandi price fluctuations and post-harvest loss continue to squeeze farm margins. Because sowing decisions often remain disconnected from market signals, bumper harvests frequently trigger farm-gate price crashes - even as India remains heavily dependent on imports for edible oils and pulses. Correcting this demand-supply mismatch requires placing market intelligence, crop diversification, warehousing and cold-chain infrastructure at the heart of agricultural planning.

Climate volatility adds another layer of urgency. Unseasonal downpours during harvest, terminal heat stress and shifting pest cycles mean that traditional calendar-based farming is no longer viable. Efficient irrigation, balanced soil nutrition, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and real-time weather advisories are now operational necessities to protect farm profitability.
Science, trust and the last mile

Agricultural innovation delivers its full value only when it reaches farmers in an actionable and accessible form. In crop protection, our guiding principle is straightforward: spray right, not spray more. Accurate pest identification, choosing the right molecules, adhering to recommended doses and timely application are vital to cutting cultivation costs while protecting crops.

For the agri-input industry, responsibility extends far beyond supplying products. Building last-mile literacy through deeper partnerships with State agricultural universities, extension networks and Krishi Vigyan Kendras can turn laboratory research into daily field practice.

Equally critical is protecting the farmers from the menace of counterfeit and sub-standard agrochemicals, which destroy both crop yields and grower trust. Eliminating spurious inputs requires a coordinated push: stricter statutory enforcement, faster state laboratory testing of all the companies and not biased sample analysis of selected companies, farmer awareness drives and end-to-end digital authentication, which includes QR-code traceability – which is mandatory across the supply chain. Simultaneously, scaling precision technologies like agricultural drones that reduce water consumption by up to 80-90 per cent and minimise applicator exposure will accelerate field-level efficiency when backed by proper training.
India’s agricultural journey over the past quarter-century secured the nation’s food bowl security. The next 25 years must strengthen the economic prosperity of those who fill it with food.

Achieving that transition requires sustained alignment among policymakers, agricultural scientists, the input industry and cultivators focused on maximising sustainable net returns per acre while safeguarding every drop of water and every inch of topsoil. Ultimately, the agricultural transformation will be judged not just by how much India grows, but also by how reliably its farmers prosper.
The author is Chairman Emeritus, Dhanuka Agritech Ltd.

title: 25 years of agricultural transformation: From Gujarat’s growth journey to farmer prosperity
